newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's job prospects to brighten, bank says.
newsitem.headline: Canada's job prospects to brighten, bank says.

text.p: Strong economic growth in Canada will shrink unemployment from its current level of 9.7 percent to 9.3 percent by the end of 1997 and to 9.0 percent by 1998, one of Canada's largest banks said on Tuesday.
The Toronto-Dominion Bank predicted that more than 270,000 net new jobs will be created both this year and next in Canada, up from less than 200,000 new jobs in 1996.
That forecast translates into roughly 30,000 net new jobs per month during the remainder of 1997, which is sharply higher than last year's pace of about 16,000 per month.
Canada's employment sagged by 18,000 jobs in February.

"Canadian employment growth is forecast to outpace U.S. employment growth over the next few years and the gap between Canadian and U.S. unemployment rates will start to narrow," said Ruth Getter, T-D Bank's chief economist.
In Canada, employment has increased by only 4.0 percent since 1990, while in the United States the number of jobs has risen by 11 percent during the same period.
Canada's unemployment rate is now more than 4.0 percentage points higher than the U.S. jobless rate of 5.3 percent.

"Employment is one of the last pieces of the puzzle to fit into place. We have seen a steady rise in productivity and competitiveness, exports have been rising at a rapid clip, corporate profits are healthy and climbing, and we have had a sharp jump in home sales in recent months," Getter said.
T-D Bank said economic growth in Canada will more than double this year to 3.3 percent, from last year's pace of 1.5 percent.
